questions.q: How does the summary define justice?
a: Something you practice daily, not something you have
A set of laws that governments enforce
A talent only a few people are born with
A reward you earn after doing good deeds
questions.why: The overview insists justice is a verb rather than a noun, a habit to improve no matter where you start.

questions.q: What three arenas does Holiday use to organize the practice of justice?
a: The Me, the We, and the All
The self, the family, and the state
The past, the present, and the future
The mind, the body, and the spirit
questions.why: The overview introduces justice as something practiced toward yourself, toward other people, and toward the whole world.

questions.q: What does the summary say about choosing your own moral code?
a: It may feel limiting at first but ultimately frees you
It should simply match whatever is legal
It should be kept private from everyone else
It is unnecessary if you follow the law
questions.why: Lesson 1 says a personal code can feel restrictive at first yet gives meaning and freedom in the long run.

questions.q: Why does the summary say justice matters more than the other virtues?
a: A person with other virtues can use them to cause harm
It is the easiest virtue to practice every day
It is the only virtue other people can see
It requires no courage or discipline at all
questions.why: Lesson 2 argues that courage, discipline or wisdom without justice can be turned toward evil and personal gain.

questions.q: What does Gandhi's example teach about justice?
a: Justice should extend to every person and living thing
Justice requires holding political office
Justice is won through armies and money
Justice is only possible for perfect people
questions.why: Lesson 3 says Gandhi's turning point was realizing that every person, animal and plant is equal.
